label: paragraph_title
text: PIRATE TO UTRAGE.

label: paragraph_title
text: “SUNNING” TOWED INTO HONG KONG.

label: text
text: CHIEF ENGINEER'S STORY.

label: paragraph_title
text: ELEVEN PIRATES KILLED.

label: text
text: How Imprisoned Officers Rushed the Bridge.

label: text
text: The pirated "Sunning" has been towed into Hong Kong after experiences which read like thrilling fiction.

label: text
text: The ship was seized on Monday afternoon by pirates from Amoy who overpowered the officers and engineers.

label: text
text: Imprisoned in the Mates' cabin six of the officers and engineers, about midnight found a revolver and 150 rounds of ammunition.

label: text
text: They determined to regain control of the ship and rushed the bridge, shooting the pirates who attempted to resist.

label: text
text: After that a running fight was kept up in the dark between the officers and the pirates.

label: text
text: Then the pirates forced the Chief Engineer to walk ahead of them up the steps of the bridge. This ruse failed and they fell back again.

label: text
text: The Chief Engineer, however, was badly injured by shots from the bridge but in spite of his wounds, joined the officers in their fight.

label: text
text: The pirates' next move was to set fire to the ship. The blaze became so big that the officers put the one European lady passenger in a boat and stood by to lower away.

label: text
text: Before dawn'some of the pirates left the ship in boats, leaving thirteen of their number to be arrested by the Navy men.

label: text
text: When daybreak came the weary officers found that some of the pirates had gone, and they were able to count the bodies of eleven killed by shots from the bridge.

label: text
text: Iater H.M.S. "Bluebell" arrived, followed by the "Suiyang" which took the "Synning" in tow.

label: paragraph_title
text: WAITING FOR "SUNNING."

label: text
text: The Tug In Heavy Seas

label: text
text: When inquiries were made in naval circles this morning, it was learned that the "Sunning" was expected to arrive about ten o'clock. However, ten o'clock came, but there was no sign of the pirated vessel. Time passed, and at noon, it was said the "Sunning" would be sighted at Waglan about one o'clock. The reason for this uncertainty was that considerable difficulty was experienced in keeping in touch with the movements of the ship, which was being towed by a tug, despatched yesterday from Taikoo, neither the disabled vessel nor the tug being fitted with wireless.

label: text
text: The tug, when sighted off Bias Bay yesterday afternoon, was proceeding slowly on account of the very heavy seas, and it was not expected that the “Sunning” was reached until late last night. Towing was extremely slow in view of the very heavy seas and the size of the ship.

label: paragraph_title
text: “SUNNING” ARRIVES.

label: paragraph_title
text: Scenes at Taikoo.

label: text
text: The "Sunning" was sighted about one o'clock by the group of newspaper men waiting at Taikoo. She was towed to the anchorage off the dock, and it was evident, even from a distance, that she had suffered badly through the flames.

label: text
text: As soon as the “Sunning” came to her moorings, about 1.45 p.m., a party of police, aboard the police launch, went on board, it is presumed to take charge of the arrested men.

label: text
text: The ambulance was waiting at Taikoo Dock, to remove the wounded Chief Engineer to hospital as soon as he could be brought ashore.

label: text
text: The “China Mail” representative at Taikoo went off to the “Sunning” in a launch, but he was not allowed to pass the gangway.

label: text
text: A police officer explained that orders had been issued by the naval officers in charge not to allow anyone aboard save the police.

label: text
text: The reporter showed his police pass, but the police officer said he was sorry, he had no authority to allow newspaper men to come aboard.

label: text
text: Invited to give some information concerning the "Sunning" the police officer said he was debarred from doing this by his instructions.

label: text
text: The reporter pointed out that not all the passengers had been accounted for, and anxiety would be allayed if some definite information could be given. The police officer, however, was unable to give any help.

label: text
text: Although not allowed on the ship, the reporter was able to note the extensive damage done by the flames.

label: text
text: The officers' and passengers' accommodation amidships appeared to have been completely gutted, and in this part of the ship there was nothing but a mass of work and charred

label: text
text: There were no boats visible on the “Sunning,” all of them being missing, either through being burnt to ashes or through being lowered away.

label: text
text: The reporter was unable to notice any of the officers or passengers on the "Sunning."

label: paragraph_title
text: "SUIYANG" ARRIVES

label: paragraph_title
text: Interview With Captain:

label: text
text: Interviewed by the “China Mail” shortly after his vessel weighed anchor, Captain P. R. Purslow, master of the a.s. “Suiyang,” stated that he first heard that there was trouble aboard the “Sunning” at 1.45 yesterday afternoon. The “Suiyang” was then just off Chelang Point.

label: text
text: His message stated that the "Sunning" had been pirated and was burning. He immediately altered his course and proceeded to the assistance of the "Sunning."

label: text
text: Continuing his graphic story of his experiences, Captain Furslow said:—"When we reached the 'Sunning' we found the vessel burning. The 'Kaying' was standing by, but upon our arrival she proceeded on her voyage and we manoeuvred in an endeavour to get into communication with the 'Sunning'.

label: text
text:
"After two or three attempts we succeeded in getting a towrope aboard the 'Sunning.' This was at 3:45 p.m. At 4:50, after heavy work, the two ships were connected and the 'Suiyang' proceeded to tow the 'Sunning' towards Hong Kong. At 5:40 the tow-rope broke. We hauled this in and again endeavoured to get a connection. It was then dark.
"We had received a wireless message stating that the Taikoo tug had left Hong Kong and I realised that the most I could do was to stand by until the tug arrived."

label: text
text: "The s.s. "Shantung" came up but I told her that there was, no need for her to wait, so she proceeded on her voyage. The "Sunning" had all equipment ready to take off passengers and crew should things get too serious. At 9.15 the tug arrived, but it was not until 11.30 that she made fast.

label: text
text:
Burning Amidships.

text: SHANGHAI WINS.

label: paragraph_title
text: Thrilling. Interport Finish.

label: text
text: VISITORS' FIGHT FOR RUNS.

label: paragraph_title
text: Local Bowlers Defied on Bad

label: text
text: Shanghai won a thrilling victory to day in the Interport ricket match against Hong Kong.

label: text
text: The finish was full of excitement.

label: text
text: On a wicket which helped the bowlers, the visitors made a desperate fight for runs and their "tail" gloriously defied the local attack.

label: paragraph_title
text: RESULTS IN PAST

label: text
text: This is the 26th Interport cricket match between Shanghai and Hong Kong.

label: text
text: Till this match began, Hong Kong had won 13 and Shanghai and one was drawn.

label: text
text: Post-war results:

label: text
text: Nov. 1920, (played at H.K.) Hong Kong won by six wickets.

label: paragraph_title
text: GREAT EXCITEMENT.

label: text
text: AMIDSF TREMENDOUS EX-CITEMENT SHANGHAI MADE THE WINNING HIT AT 2.45 P.M. GAINING THE VERDICT BY ONE WICKET.

label: text
text: May, 1921, (at Shanghai), Shanghai won by an innings and 159 runs.

label: text
text: Nov., 1922. (at H.K.), Shanghai won by 2 wickets.

label: text
text: May. 1923, (at Shanghai), Hong Kong won by 3 Vickets. Nov., 1924, (at H.K.), Hong Kong won by an innings and runs.

label: text
text: May, 1925, (at Shanghai), Hong Kong won by 7 runs.

label: text
text: With 4 wickets in hand, the local side started 86 runs on (score: 97, Ramsay-20 not out, Parker 2 not out).

label: text
text: The big roller was put on and had the effect of making the wicket less difficult to begin with. Ramsay faced Leach (Law Courts end) and ran a leg bye off the first ball.

label: text
text: The next delivery dismissed Parker. It pitched a little short and the batsman played forward to it, giving Barnes, the wicketkeeper, an easy catch. (98-7-2).

label: text

label: text
text: Ramsay continued to bat with confidence, watching O'Hara very carefully.

label: text

label: paragraph_title
text: WORTHY CAUSE.

label: text
text: SERVICES APPEAL FOR BLIND

label: text
text: "A GREAT STEP FORWARD"

label: text
text: The Colonial Secretary sends the "China Mail" a copy of the following letter:—

label: text
text:
224. Great Portland Street, Services' Appeal in aid of:—
1. Blind ex-service men not eligible for a Government Pension or training at St. Dunham's.
2. Ex-service men who become blind after reversion to civil life.

label: text
text: All serving or ex-service men's wives or children who are or may become so afflicted.

label: text
text: 9th October, 1926.

label: text
text: Firstly, we would like to thank all those who supported this Appeal last year, especially those who became Annual Subscribers.

label: text
text: Under the three categories mentioned above, help has been rendered. In addition, many men now serving are receiving assistance in respect of their blind relations.

label: text
text: In the administration of this Fund a great step forward has been made. The Fund now co-operates with Regimental Associations, thus the applicants have not only received expert assistance more quickly, but in many cases overlapping has been avoided.

label: text
text: For these reasons and because of the fact that owing to the Strike and the increase of unemployment, many who have formerly assisted the Fund are now unable to do so, we have no hesitation in asking you to combine to support the Fund. We may add that we rely mainly on those men who are actually drawing pay.

label: text
text: Many men are still being trained and several are already earning their own living. Although funds are not yet sufficient to give actual pensions to old and infirm men not capable of being trained, regular financial relief is in some cases being given.

label: text
text:
Each case comes under the per-
acnal supervision of Captain E. B. R. Towse, whose experience is in-
valuable.

label: text
text: Contributions should be sent to Captain E. B. B. Towse, V.C., C.B.E., at 224, Great Portland Street, W.1.

label: paragraph_title
text: Yours faithfully,

label: text
text:
(Sd.) Allenby, Field Marshal.
(Sd.) Wm. Robertson, Field Marshal.

label: paragraph_title
text: TWO MORE SHIPS.

label: paragraph_title
text: TO-DAY'S MAIDEN TRIP.

label: paragraph_title
text: Big Shipment Brought Down

label: text
text: Material improvement has to be recorded in trade between Canton and Hong Kong, following the cessation of the "new" boycott or discrimination against British shipping.

label: text
text: The most significant development to record to-day is the addition of two vessels to the trade.

label: text
text: One is the "new steamboat "Yuet On," built locally and now running under the Chinese flag. She sailed for Canton this morning on her maiden trip.

label: text
text: The other is a coastal freighter, being the ex-Douglas ship "Haimun," now also under Chinese registry. She is to make bi-weekly sailings between Hong Kong and Canton for freight.

label: paragraph_title
text: British Goods

label: text
text: As indicated yesterday, the working of cargo on British ships is not expected to begin till next week, as there are many lesser arrangements to make in the interval.

label: text
text: Yesterday the s.s. "Kwong Sai" took down about 150 tons of cargo—the biggest shipment on a steamboat since the "new" boy-cott was inaugurated on November 8.

label: text
text: One effect of the cancellation of the Transport Union's boycott resolution has been the pronounced improvement in tone in Canton business circles.

label: text
text: Only a prejudiced minority, with their own interests to serve, are agitating for fixing a date to liquidate stocks of British goods.

label: text
text: The four Chambers of Commerce have been silent on the matter for at least a week.

label: text
text: A contributory cause to the delay in resumption of normal goods communications is the request put

label: text
text: forward by employees of the Maritime Customs brokers that patrons be charged an additional 1 per cent. for their bonus, the present 1 per cent. commission going entirely to the brokers themselves.

label: text
text: It is anticipated that the merchants will pay

label: text
text: In Kongmoon, merchants, in addition to paying the new special taxes, are going to further expense in satisfying the rival claims of the Cargo Coolies and Cargo Boatmen.

label: paragraph_title
text: ON WEST RIVER.

label: paragraph_title
text: Congestion Clearing Up: Searchers Ignored.

label: text
text:
[From Our Own Correspondent.]
Samshui (West River), Nov. 14.
River steamers under the British flag (i.e. those which do not submit to searches by the Canton Inspection Corps) are still ignoring the examination pontoon at Do-sing (one of the West River ports below Wuchow).

label: text
text: If there is cargo on board for that port, the procedure is to go straight on to the place for discharge. If there are neither passengers nor cargo at that intermediate port, the boats go straight on.

label: text
text: A Hong Kong-Wuchow vessel under the Chinese flag has been delayed at Wuchow owing to the Firemen's Union and the Seamen's Union putting in demands.

label: text
text: The congestion of merchandise at Wuchow is now easing up but there is still cattle in abundance for export to Hong Kong.
